title: Iran and the U.S. Just Traded Air Strikes. India's ₹100 Petrol Is About to Get Worse.
excerpt: Oil surged 3% after the IRGC hit a U.S. airbase in retaliation for American strikes near Bandar Abbas. For India, which imports 85% of its crude, the three-month-old war just entered a new and more dangerous phase.
body:
The fragile ceasefire between the United States and Iran, barely seven weeks old, came closer to collapse on Thursday than at any point since it was brokered in early April.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it struck an American airbase — location undisclosed — at 4:50 a.m. local time, in retaliation for what it described as a U.S. attack near Bandar Abbas airport hours earlier. The Pentagon confirmed it had shot down four Iranian attack drones near the Strait of Hormuz and struck a ground control station in the port city that was "about to launch a fifth drone."

"These actions were measured, purely defensive and intended to maintain the ceasefire," a U.S. official told Reuters on condition of anonymity.

The IRGC, however, warned that "any repeat of this aggression would draw a more decisive response," and said responsibility for consequences lay with "the aggressor."

What Happened

The sequence began when U.S. Central Command detected what it described as an Iranian drone operation threatening American forces and commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. The military intercepted four one-way attack drones and hit the ground station controlling them near Bandar Abbas.

Iran retaliated within hours, targeting the American base from which the strike on Bandar Abbas was launched. Kuwait, which hosts a major U.S. installation, said it was responding to missile and drone attacks without naming the source. Israel, engaged in its own operations against Hezbollah in southern Lebanon, sounded air raid sirens over hostile aircraft activity in the north.

The exchange is the most direct military confrontation between Washington and Tehran since the ceasefire took effect, and it happened on the same day Trump dismissed an Iranian state TV report of a draft deal that would have restored commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz within a month, with Iran and Oman jointly managing traffic.

"Nobody's going to control the strait," Trump said at a cabinet meeting. "It's international waters and Oman will behave just like everybody else or we'll have to blow them up."

Why India Cannot Look Away

The strategic arithmetic is brutal for New Delhi. India imports roughly 85 percent of its crude oil, and the Strait of Hormuz — which handled a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas traffic before the war — remains effectively closed to normal commercial shipping three months into the conflict.

Oil prices, which had fallen more than 5 percent on Wednesday on deal hopes, surged over 3 percent after the strikes. U.S. crude futures led the rebound while global equities fell and the dollar rose.

The impact is already visible on Indian streets. Petrol crossed ₹100 per litre in most Indian cities last week after the fourth fuel price hike in two weeks. IndiGo and Air India have cut up to 22 percent of domestic flights as jet fuel costs become unsustainable. The Reserve Bank of India's growth forecasts for fiscal 2027 are under revision.

Foreign investors have already pulled $23 billion out of Indian equities this year, and the Nifty 50 is headed for its first annual decline since 2015 — driven in significant part by the war's inflation overhang.

The Deal That Isn't

The Iranian state TV report that Trump dismissed described a framework in which the U.S. would lift its blockade of Iranian ports, withdraw military forces from Iran's vicinity, and allow Iran and Oman to jointly manage Hormuz traffic. The White House called it a "complete fabrication."

The sticking points remain the same three issues that have blocked progress since March: the Strait of Hormuz's operating framework, the dismantling of Iran's nuclear capacity, and the lifting of U.S. sanctions. Iranian officials have said nuclear talks will come in a second round — a sequencing that may not be acceptable to Washington's hawks.

"The bottom line is Iran's never going to have a nuclear weapon," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said at the same cabinet meeting.

What This Means for NRIs

For the Indian diaspora, the Iran war's effects have been pervasive and personal. Higher crude prices feed directly into remittance calculations as the rupee weakens. Airfares between India and the U.S., already elevated by post-pandemic demand, have risen further as airlines pass on fuel surcharges. And the broader macroeconomic damage — slower growth, higher inflation, a falling stock market — erodes the value of NRI investments in Indian equities and real estate.

The war has no visible off-ramp. Trump says a deal is close. Iran says it will not back down on uranium enrichment or Hormuz control. And India, which is not at the negotiating table, is paying the price at the pump.
